lessons.title: Chemical cells and fuel cells
lessons.summary: See how two different metals in an electrolyte make a voltage, why some batteries can be recharged and others cannot, and how a hydrogen fuel cell turns fuel into electricity.
objectives: I can describe how a simple cell is made from two different metals and an electrolyte.
I can explain how the difference in reactivity of the metals affects the voltage of a cell.
I can describe the difference between rechargeable and non-rechargeable batteries.
I can describe how a hydrogen fuel cell works and evaluate its advantages and disadvantages.
I can write the half equations for a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell (Higher).

activities.title: Making electricity from a reaction
activities.content:
## A simple cell

A **cell** turns chemical energy into electrical energy. All you need is:

- **Two different metals** (the electrodes), and
- an **electrolyte** (a solution containing ions, such as salt water or dilute acid) that the metals dip into.

Connect the two metals with a wire and a current flows.

### Why does it work?

The more reactive metal wants to lose electrons and form ions more than the less reactive metal does. So electrons are pushed out of the more reactive metal, along the wire, into the less reactive one. That flow of electrons **is** the current. The electrolyte completes the circuit by letting ions move between the electrodes.

A lemon with a zinc nail and a copper coin stuck in it is a working (if feeble) cell. The lemon juice is the electrolyte.

### A battery

A **battery** is two or more cells joined together **in series**. The voltages add up, which is how a 9 V battery can be built from six 1.5 V cells.

Many people call a single cell a "battery", but in your exam keep the terms separate.

activities.title: Worked example: predicting the voltage
activities.content:
**A student sets up cells using different pairs of metals in sodium chloride solution and records the voltage.**

| Metals | Voltage (V) |
|---|---|
| magnesium and copper | 1.8 |
| zinc and copper | 1.1 |
| iron and copper | 0.6 |
| copper and copper | 0.0 |

**What pattern is there?**

The **bigger the difference in reactivity** between the two metals, the **bigger the voltage**. Magnesium is much more reactive than copper, so that pair gives the highest reading. Iron is only a little more reactive than copper, so the voltage is small.

Two identical metals give **no voltage at all**, because neither metal has any tendency to push electrons towards the other.

**Predict the voltage for magnesium and zinc.**

Magnesium is more reactive than zinc, but they are closer together than magnesium and copper. A sensible estimate is 1.8 − 1.1 = **about 0.7 V**.

**Other things that change the voltage:** the type of electrolyte and its concentration also matter, so keep them the same when comparing metals.

question.text: Which pair of metals would give the largest voltage when used as electrodes in the same electrolyte?
question.hint: Look for the pair that is furthest apart in the reactivity series.
question.explanation: Magnesium is high in the reactivity series and silver is very low, so they have the largest difference and give the biggest voltage.

options.feedback: These are close together in the reactivity series, so the voltage is small.

question.text: Complete the sentences about a simple cell.

metadata.blanksText: A simple cell needs two ___ metals and an electrolyte. Electrons flow from the more ___ metal through the wire. A battery is made of two or more cells connected in ___.

question.hint: The metals must not be the same. Think about which metal loses electrons most easily.
question.explanation: The two metals must be different; electrons leave the more reactive metal; cells joined in series make a battery.

activities.title: Rechargeable or not?
activities.content:
## Why batteries go flat

A cell only produces a voltage while the chemical reaction inside it is happening. Once one of the reactants is **used up**, the reaction stops and the cell is **flat**.

### Non-rechargeable cells

In ordinary **alkaline batteries** (the AA and AAA cells in a remote control) the reactions are **not reversible**. When the chemicals have been used up, the cell has to be thrown away or recycled. Trying to force a current through it does not restore the original chemicals.

### Rechargeable cells

In a **rechargeable** cell, such as the lithium-ion cell in a phone or the lead–acid battery in a car, the reactions **can be reversed**. Connecting the cell to an external electrical supply pushes the current the other way and turns the products back into the original reactants. The cell can then be used again.

### Comparing them

| | Non-rechargeable | Rechargeable |
|---|---|---|
| Reaction | irreversible | reversible with external current |
| Cost per use | cheap to buy, expensive over time | more expensive to buy, cheaper over many uses |
| Waste | thrown away when flat | reused hundreds of times |

Neither type lasts for ever. Rechargeable cells slowly lose capacity, which is why an old phone battery does not hold its charge.

question.text: True or false: a non-rechargeable cell stops working because the reaction inside it is reversible.
question.hint: Think about why the chemicals cannot be restored.
question.explanation: False. It stops because a reactant has been used up, and the reaction is irreversible so it cannot be recharged.

activities.title: Hydrogen fuel cells
activities.content:
## A cell that never goes flat while you feed it

A **fuel cell** is different from an ordinary cell: instead of using up chemicals sealed inside, it is supplied with a **fuel** and **oxygen** (usually from the air) continuously from outside. As long as the fuel keeps flowing, it keeps producing electricity.

The most important example is the **hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell**. The fuel is hydrogen, and it is oxidised inside the cell to make water and release electrical energy.

**Overall reaction:** 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

This is exactly the same as burning hydrogen. The difference is that in a fuel cell the energy is released as **electricity** rather than as heat and light. The only product is **water**.

### Inside the cell

- Hydrogen enters at the **negative electrode**, where it loses electrons.
- Oxygen enters at the **positive electrode**, where it gains electrons.
- The electrons travel through the external circuit from the negative to the positive electrode, powering a motor or light.
- Ions travel through the electrolyte between the electrodes to complete the circuit.

### Half equations (Higher)

Negative electrode (oxidation): **2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻**

Positive electrode (reduction): **O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O**

Add them together and the H⁺ ions and electrons cancel, leaving 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

activities.title: Worked example: fuel cell car or battery car?
activities.content:
**A car company is choosing between hydrogen fuel cells and rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. Evaluate the two options.**

**Advantages of the fuel cell**

- Refuelling with hydrogen takes a few minutes; recharging a battery can take hours.
- Fuel cells are lighter than the large batteries needed for a long range.
- The only product from the cell is water, so no pollution at the point of use.
- Fewer toxic metals to dispose of at the end of the car's life.

**Disadvantages of the fuel cell**

- Hydrogen is a flammable gas and must be stored under high pressure, which needs strong, heavy tanks.
- There are very few hydrogen filling stations.
- Most hydrogen is currently made from natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide, so the fuel is only "clean" if made by electrolysis using renewable electricity.
- Fuel cells are still expensive and contain platinum catalysts.

**A balanced conclusion** would say that fuel cells suit long-range or heavy vehicles, while batteries currently suit shorter journeys with easy home charging. The examiner wants both sides and then a judgement.

question.text: Which statements about a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about what goes in, what comes out, and whether it needs recharging.
question.explanation: The fuel cell produces only water and does not need recharging because hydrogen is supplied continuously. Hydrogen is oxidised, not reduced, and it is a gas that is hard to store, not a liquid.

options.text: The only chemical product is water.
It does not run down as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied.
Hydrogen is reduced at the negative electrode.
options.feedback: Hydrogen loses electrons at the negative electrode, which is oxidation.

options.text: Hydrogen is easy to store because it is a liquid at room temperature.
options.feedback: Hydrogen is a gas and must be stored under high pressure.

question.text: Match each type of cell to the correct description.
question.hint: One is thrown away, one is reversed with a current, one is fed from outside.
question.explanation: Alkaline cells are non-rechargeable; lithium-ion cells are recharged by reversing the reaction; fuel cells are supplied continuously with fuel and oxygen.

pairs.right: reaction reversed by applying an external current
fuel and oxygen supplied continuously from outside

activities.title: Checking half equations (Higher)
activities.content:
## Balancing the fuel cell equations

Students often get the fuel cell half equations muddled, so here is how to check them.

**Negative electrode:** 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻

- Atoms: 4 H on the left, 4 H on the right. Balanced.
- Charge: 0 on the left; (4+) + (4−) = 0 on the right. Balanced.
- Electrons on the **right**, so this is **oxidation**. Hydrogen is the fuel being oxidised.

**Positive electrode:** O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O

- Atoms: 2 O and 4 H on both sides. Balanced.
- Charge: (4+) + (4−) = 0 on the left; 0 on the right. Balanced.
- Electrons on the **left**, so this is **reduction**.

**Adding them:** the 4H⁺ and 4e⁻ appear on opposite sides and cancel out, giving

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

Some exam boards write the equations for an alkaline electrolyte using OH⁻ ions instead, but the acid version above is the one to learn for AQA.

**Direction of electrons in the wire:** from the negative electrode (where they are released) to the positive electrode (where they are used).

question.text:
A bus company is considering replacing its diesel buses with buses powered by hydrogen fuel cells.

(a) Write the overall equation for the reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell.

(b) Give two advantages of using hydrogen fuel cells rather than diesel engines.

(c) Give two disadvantages of hydrogen fuel cells.

(d) **Higher tier:** Write the half equation for the reaction at the negative electrode.
question.hint: Think about the product of the fuel cell, how hydrogen is stored and produced, and where the electrons come from.
question.explanation: (a) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. (b) The only product is water, so no carbon dioxide or particulates at the point of use; quieter; hydrogen can be made from renewable electricity. (c) Hydrogen is flammable and must be stored at high pressure; few refuelling stations; most hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels; fuel cells are expensive. (d) 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

markScheme.criterion: Advantage 1: only product is water / no carbon dioxide or pollutants released
Advantage 2: any other valid point (quiet, hydrogen can be made using renewable energy, no toxic battery metals)
Two disadvantages: hydrogen is flammable / difficult to store, few filling stations, hydrogen often made from fossil fuels, expensive

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- A **cell** = two **different** metals + an **electrolyte**. Electrons flow from the more reactive metal.
- **Bigger difference in reactivity → bigger voltage.** Same metals → 0 V. The electrolyte also affects the voltage.
- A **battery** is cells connected in series.
- **Non-rechargeable** cells (alkaline) stop when a reactant is used up; the reaction is irreversible.
- **Rechargeable** cells can be reversed by an external current.
- A **fuel cell** is fed fuel and oxygen continuously. The hydrogen fuel cell gives **2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O** and only produces water.
- Higher: negative electrode **2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻** (oxidation); positive electrode **O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O** (reduction).
- Pros: clean at the point of use, quick to refuel. Cons: hydrogen storage, safety, production from fossil fuels, cost.

practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how a 9 V battery is built from 1.5 V cells.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A battery is two or more cells connected in series so that their voltages add together.

options.text: Two or more cells connected in series
A single cell with a large voltage
Two identical metals in an electrolyte

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: the only chemical product of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is water.
practiceQuestions.hint: What do you get when hydrogen combines with oxygen?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, so water is the only product.

practiceQuestions.text: A torch battery is made from four cells, each producing 1.5 V, connected in series. What is the total voltage of the battery in volts?
A student makes a cell using two copper strips in sodium chloride solution. Which reading would the voltmeter show?
practiceQuestions.hint: Do the two electrodes differ in reactivity?
practiceQuestions.explanation: With identical metals there is no difference in reactivity, so no electrons are pushed round the circuit and the voltage is zero.

options.text: It depends on the size of the strips

practiceQuestions.text: Metal pairs are tested in the same electrolyte with copper always as one electrode. Put the other metals in order from the one giving the LOWEST voltage to the one giving the HIGHEST.
practiceQuestions.hint: The further the metal is from copper in the reactivity series, the higher the voltage.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Iron is closest to copper (lowest voltage), then zinc, then magnesium, then calcium (highest).

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier. Complete the half equation for the positive electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell.
practiceQuestions.hint: Balance the oxygen atoms first, then the charge.
practiceQuestions.explanation: One O₂ gives two water molecules; 4H⁺ carry 4+ charge, so 4 electrons are needed to balance to zero.

practiceQuestions.text: Which factors affect the voltage produced by a simple cell? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two are about the metals and the electrolyte; two are not.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The difference in reactivity of the two metals and the type of electrolyte both affect the voltage. The length of the wire and the colour of the beaker do not.

options.text: The difference in reactivity between the two metals
The length of the connecting wire
options.feedback: Wire length affects resistance slightly but not the voltage the cell produces.

practiceQuestions.text: In a hydrogen fuel cell, 0.2 mol of hydrogen gas reacts completely. Use the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O to calculate the mass of water produced in grams. (Mr of H₂O = 18)
practiceQuestions.hint: The ratio of H₂ to H₂O is 2 : 2, so the moles are equal.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 0.2 mol H₂ gives 0.2 mol H₂O. mass = 0.2 × 18 = 3.6 g.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why an alkaline cell eventually stops producing a voltage, and why it cannot simply be recharged.
practiceQuestions.hint: What happens to the reactants, and is the reaction reversible?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cell stops when one of the reactants has been used up so the reaction can no longer happen. The reaction is irreversible, so passing a current through it does not regenerate the reactants.

markScheme.criterion: A reactant is used up so the reaction stops
The reaction is not reversible / cannot be reversed by an external current

practiceQuestions.text:
A student investigates how the voltage of a cell depends on the metals used. She uses copper as one electrode each time and changes the other metal, keeping the electrolyte the same.

(a) State the independent variable and one control variable in this investigation.

(b) Explain why the voltage is highest when magnesium is used as the second electrode.

(c) Suggest why a cell using magnesium and copper would not be suitable for powering a device for a long time.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what she changes, what she keeps the same, and what happens to a reactive metal in an electrolyte over time.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Independent: the metal used for the second electrode. Control: the electrolyte (type and concentration), or the size of the electrodes, or the distance between them. (b) Magnesium is much more reactive than copper, and the greater the difference in reactivity, the greater the voltage. (c) Magnesium is very reactive so it corrodes or reacts with the electrolyte quickly and is used up, so the cell goes flat.

markScheme.criterion: Independent variable: the type of metal used as the second electrode
Control variable: electrolyte (type/concentration/volume), electrode size, distance apart, or temperature
Magnesium has the greatest difference in reactivity from copper, and a bigger difference gives a bigger voltage
Magnesium reacts / corrodes / is used up quickly so the cell goes flat

practiceQuestions.text: Four cells are made using the same electrolyte but different pairs of metal electrodes. Which pair would give the SMALLEST voltage?
practiceQuestions.hint: The voltage depends on how far apart the two metals are in the reactivity series.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Iron and zinc are next to each other in the reactivity series, so the difference in reactivity is small and the voltage is low. The other pairs combine a reactive metal with a very unreactive one, giving larger voltages.

options.feedback: Magnesium is far more reactive than copper, so this pair gives a large voltage.
Silver is very low in the reactivity series, so the gap from zinc is large.
These are at opposite ends of the reactivity series and give the biggest voltage of all.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about how a simple cell works.

metadata.blanksText: The two metal electrodes are dipped into an ___, a solution that contains ions and conducts electricity. The greater the difference in ___ between the two metals, the larger the voltage. The voltage is measured by connecting a ___ between the two electrodes.

practiceQuestions.hint: The solution has a special name; the metals are compared using the reactivity series; the meter measures volts.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The solution is the electrolyte; the voltage depends on the difference in reactivity of the metals; a voltmeter measures the potential difference between them.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a rechargeable cell can be recharged because the chemical reaction inside it can be reversed by passing an electric current through it from an external source.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what 'recharging' actually does to the chemicals inside the cell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. In a rechargeable cell the reaction is reversible, so an external current drives the reaction backwards and restores the original reactants.

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements about hydrogen fuel cells are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider what happens to the hydrogen inside the cell, where the hydrogen comes from, and what the cell gives out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hydrogen loses electrons at the negative electrode, so it is oxidised. Hydrogen has to be manufactured first, usually by electrolysis or from natural gas, so a fuel cell is not a primary source of energy. The only product is water, and a fuel cell does not store electricity; it generates it while fuel is supplied.

options.text: Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode.
The hydrogen has to be manufactured first, for example by electrolysis of water.
The fuel cell gives out carbon dioxide while it is working.
options.feedback: The only chemical product of a hydrogen fuel cell is water.

options.text: A fuel cell stores electrical energy in the same way as a lithium-ion battery.
options.feedback: A fuel cell does not store energy; it produces a voltage only while hydrogen and oxygen are being supplied.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each device to the description of how its cell works.
practiceQuestions.hint: One cell cannot be reversed, one is reversed by an external current, and one is fed with fuel from outside.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A zinc–carbon torch cell is non-rechargeable and is thrown away once a reactant is used up. An electric car battery uses lithium-ion cells whose reactions are reversed by charging. A fuel cell bus is supplied continuously with hydrogen and oxygen and produces only water.

pairs.right: irreversible reaction, thrown away when a reactant is used up

pairs.left: lithium-ion battery in an electric car
pairs.right: reaction reversed by an external current during charging

pairs.left: fuel cell in a hydrogen bus
pairs.right: hydrogen and oxygen supplied continuously, producing only water

practiceQuestions.text:
A car manufacturer is deciding whether to power a new electric car with a hydrogen fuel cell or a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

(a) Write the overall equation for the reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell.

(b) Give two advantages of using a hydrogen fuel cell rather than a rechargeable battery.

(c) Give two disadvantages of hydrogen fuel cells.

(d) **Higher tier:** Write the half equation for the reaction at the positive electrode.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the fuel cell produces, how long each option takes to refill or recharge, how hydrogen is stored and made, and what oxygen does at the positive electrode.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. (b) The only product is water; a fuel cell can be refilled with hydrogen in minutes whereas a battery takes much longer to recharge; fuel cells do not contain toxic metals such as those in some batteries and do not degrade over many charge cycles; hydrogen can be made using renewable electricity. (c) Hydrogen is flammable and has to be stored as a gas at high pressure; there are few hydrogen filling stations; most hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels; fuel cells are expensive. (d) O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.

markScheme.criterion: Advantage 1: only product is water / no carbon dioxide or pollutants released
Advantage 2: any other valid point (quick to refill, no toxic battery metals, does not wear out with charge cycles, hydrogen can be made using renewable energy)
Two disadvantages: hydrogen is flammable / difficult to store, few filling stations, hydrogen often made from fossil fuels, expensive
